newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-No quick fix for Australian jobless.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-No quick fix for Australian jobless.

text.p: Australian Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone has ruled out finding a quick fix for lowering Australia's unemployment rate, which seems reluctant to budge from around the 8.5 percent level recorded in recent months.

Speaking a year after the Liberal-National coalition was elected to government, Vanstone said she had achieved all she had aimed to in her first year in the ministry, but unemployment would continue to be a blight.
"Labor really has left us with, I think it's fair to say, an ingrained stain on the economy," Vanstone told Reuters.
"There's no Dynamo (detergent) fix -- no little on the stain and the rest in the wash and out it all comes -- it is an ingrained stain and we take it as a very high priority."

Vanstone said the government faced the challenge of policy reforms to cut the unemployment rate, adding that the Labor Party and the Australian Democrats were the biggest obstacle to reducing unemployment.
Labor and Democrat opposition in the upper house Senate to most government reforms meant the passage of legislation relied on two independent senators.
"I think the Australian people are watching very carefully what we do," Vanstone said.
"We were elected to fix the mess and they want to know that we're working on it -- they'll judge us very harshly if we don't."
One of her colleagues, Liberal backbencher Bill Taylor, recently nominated the "unacceptably high level of unemployment" as the top priority for the government in its second year.
In its mid-year economic review released in January, the government forecast an unemployment rate of 8.5 percent for the June quarter of the 1996/97 financial year.
The forecast was revised up from a previous target of 8.25 percent. The jobless rate was at 8.6 percent in January 1997 and has been stuck at or above 8.5 percent for most of 1996.
Taylor said it was not unreasonable for Australians to expect some improvement over the next 12 months.
But Vanstone, who early last year said the coalition would lose the next election if it failed to cut unemployment, said she believed voters knew the problem would not vanish overnight.
"What they are looking for is the real changes to be made," she said. "They understand what sort of a mess it is and they understand that it isn't an overnight fix."
"They are watching carefully to see that we are prepared to make the tough decisions."
However, she again refused to set an unemployment rate target, saying it would only distract the government from the challenge of making the necessary policy changes.

She said Australians also realised the government's plans to return the budget to surplus, to boost business confidence and free up the labour market were all aimed at pulling the unemployment rate down.
"If you look at a list of countries with lower unemployment, it's a fair bet that they've got a fairly flexible labour market," she said.
"There's enormous flexibility there (with the industrial relations changes) -- it's just got to be picked up and used."
The Australian parliament last year passed the government's workplace reforms, which aim to deregulate the labour market and give unions a less significant role in wage negotiations.
